props.title: Triumph of the Will

sections.content: **Triumph of the Will** (1935) stands as one of cinema's most controversial masterpieces - a brilliant propaganda film that served evil ends. Director Leni Riefenstahl revolutionized documentary techniques through dramatic angles, tracking shots, and masterful editing that influenced filmmakers for decades after. The massive scale of the Nuremberg rally sequences, with hundreds of thousands of participants filmed from multiple vantage points, established visual patterns that echo through films like **Star Wars** (1977) and **The Lion King** (1994). Yet its explicit purpose as Nazi propaganda makes it impossible to separate the technical innovations from its sinister agenda.

sections.content: The ethical debate around **Triumph of the Will** (1935) influenced how later documentarians approached political subjects. **The Sorrow and the Pity** (1969) deliberately used rough, unpolished footage to document French collaboration with Nazis, rejecting Riefenstahl's glossy aesthetics. **Night and Fog** (1956) by Alain Resnais confronted concentration camp reality head-on, serving as a stark counterpoint to Riefenstahl's idealized Reich. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Documentary Film

Contemporary documentary filmmakers like Errol Morris in **The Fog of War** (2003) and Joshua Oppenheimer in **The Act of Killing** (2012) grapple with how to depict political violence and complicity without glorification. Their work shows an acute awareness of **Triumph's** cautionary legacy about the power of documentary film to shape historical narrative. Even technically brilliant works like **Olympia** (1938), Riefenstahl's follow-up documentary about the 1936 Berlin Olympics, remain inseparable from their propagandistic context.
